note: Fe's half of the Phase 0 manifest (00b-oracle-and-differential-corpus.md). kg owns the sibling test/lisp-compat/features.json (sub-plan 00C); the two id spaces must not collide, checked by utils/check_compat_manifest.py. This file intentionally holds only the handful of entries needed to prove the mechanism -- populating the corpus is 00C's job, not this one's.

features.rationale: Fe's error text already carries Emacs' condition name ('void-function <symbol>'), by design (see fe.c's HandleNonCallable/HandleVoidSymbol comments), but until Phase 6 it is prose in FeHandleError()'s message rather than a structured, catchable condition object. Every recorded Fe-side record for this feature carries condition_source: "message" for exactly that reason.

Fe has no hash-table type, no reader syntax for one, and no primitives that construct or query one. Not on this program's roadmap; the compat runner short-circuits cases naming this feature instead of running them and pattern-matching an unbound-symbol error that would look identical to a real gap.

Fe has no signal primitive and no condition hierarchy; both arrive with Phase 6 (parent plan section 6, 'Introduce structured completion and non-local control'). Until then Fe reports an ordinary void-function condition instead of the quit Emacs raises for (signal 'quit nil); this is deliberately not a required-match feature yet, so run-fe-compat.py reports the gap without failing the corpus over it.

Emacs's plain (non-cl-lib) namespace does not define `assert` at all under `emacs -Q --batch`; Fe's `assert` is a core primitive with no direct oracle analogue by this name. Recorded as divergent rather than kg-policy because the disagreement is meaningfully demonstrated by a real oracle snapshot (void-function), not merely undemonstrable.

Emacs has no `env` primitive bound in `emacs -Q --batch`; Fe's `env` is a core introspection primitive returning the interpreter's whole current symbol list (fe.c's PEnv arm), a Fe-specific capability with no Emacs analogue by this name.

Same name, incompatible shape: Emacs's `let` takes a bindings list as its first argument and signals wrong-type-argument when given a bare symbol; Fe's `let` takes a bare symbol directly and has no separate body argument at all. kg's prelude `let` macro (tracked in kg's own manifest, owner kg, comparison emacs) is the Emacs-shaped construct; this entry is Fe's distinct low-level primitive.

Return-value divergence only; the mutation itself (CAR becomes 9) is not independently observable through this case's shared single-expression protocol, but the printed return value already demonstrates the disagreement.
Return-value divergence, same root cause as primitive-setcar: fe.c's PSetCdr arm never assigns its `res` return value.

The 04D namespace cut, as recorded: the bootstrap moved into function cells and the value-cell call-position fallback was deleted, so the primitive `car`'s value cell is empty and `(boundp 'car)` is nil -- the Lisp-2 answer this snapshot has pinned since 00C. The pre-cut Fe reported t because a single value cell held both the primitive and any value of that name; the cut is what flipped the answer.

Sub-plan 04D: `#'x` now reads as `(function x)` -- Read's `#` case routes through the same ReadWrapped construction `quote` uses, with `stray '#''` kept for a bare `#'` -- and the writer prints `(function X)` as `#'X` the way Emacs' printer does, so `(quote #'car)` reads as `(quote (function car))` and prints `#'car`. The pre-cut reader treated `#'` as identity, and its own historical rationale (a stale fe.c line number in the pre-cut tree) described that gap.

Parent plan section 2's numeric model ('Add: signed 64-bit integers; existing floating-point values') is Phase 5, not yet implemented; fe.c has exactly one FeTNumber double representation today, and its writer (EmitDouble) special-cases integral values to omit the fractional part -- matching Emacs' printed form for genuine integers by coincidence, and diverging from it for floats that happen to be integral. This is one of the plan's named day-one divergences ('No integers. 42 and 42.0 are the same object and print the same.').

Deliberately not implemented: FeReadFn (fe.h's public read callback) yields one raw byte at a time with no lookahead buffer for multi-byte reassembly at the reader's character-literal site, so `?Ã©` (a two-byte UTF-8 encoding) would read only its first byte -- exactly the silent wrongness this compat manifest exists to prevent. Failing clearly (void-variable on the resulting bare symbol) is the current, intentional behavior rather than a bug to fix; a real implementation needs the reader's byte source to support decoding a full codepoint, which is untracked.

Parent plan section 7 ('Make strict arity normal') is Phase 7, milestone 2, not yet implemented or funded by this slice's Decision. Fe's `-a`/`fe -a` strict-arity pass exists standalone (test.sh's third pass) but is opt-in, not the evaluator's default -- this entry tracks the *default* mode's behavior, which is what an ordinary `(lambda ...)` call site sees.

This is the parent plan's own example of a divergence-from-Fe that is an agreement-with-Emacs: kg's fe fork changed vanilla Fe's historical behavior (silently returning nil for an unbound symbol) specifically to match Emacs's void-variable signal, and doc/fe-upstream.md's divergence table records that as a deliberate, already-landed change, not a Phase 2+ item. Status is `supported` because the oracle comparison is what this manifest tracks; the vanilla-Fe distinction is prose context only, not a comparison axis this schema has a field for.

This is kg/fe's own deliberate policy, not an Emacs contract: the parent kg repository's CLAUDE.md already states the precedent for exactly this shape of decision (kg_regex_match_backward's backward-matching policy is kg's own, not Emacs', so an oracle for it would have to encode kg's policy rather than read Emacs'), and 00b-oracle-and-differential-corpus.md's own 'What this does not do' names cyclic-structure printing explicitly. Pinned by fe/test_api.c's TestWriter, which already asserts all three bounded forms (#<cycle>, #<deep>, #<truncated>).

Sub-plan 02B lands `setq` as a core special form (fe.c's EvaluateSetq, reached from EvaluatePrimitive's PSetq arm): pair iteration over the existing assignment path, updating the innermost lexical binding when one exists and the global value cell otherwise. Sub-plan 02C then deleted the historical assignment `=` it landed beside, so `setq` is Fe's only assignment special form and `=` is numeric equality (primitive-numeric-eq).

Sub-plan 02B lands `set` (fe.c's EvaluateSet, reached from EvaluatePrimitive's PSet arm) as an ordinary, exact-arity function using the existing global setter FeSet() -- it always writes the symbol's global value cell and never reads or changes a lexical binding of the same spelling, unlike `setq`.

Sub-plan 02C repurposes `=` as numeric equality over Fe's existing doubles (fe.c's EvaluateNumericEqual, reached from EvaluatePrimitive's PNumericEqual arm, formerly the assignment primitive PAssign/primitive-assign-eq, now deleted): a left-to-right chained comparison, at least one argument required, every argument form evaluated left to right before any value is type-checked, and every operand validated and compared without short-circuiting once the result is already known. Phase 5 later extends this to integers/mixed types without redefining it, so these cases are written to leave room for that.

Sub-plan 04C, the phase's headline: a symbol holds a value (7) and a function (an fset'd lambda) at once, call position resolves the function cell, bare-symbol evaluation the value cell, and (list f (f)) is (7 9). 04D then moved the bootstrap into function cells and deleted the value-cell fallback; this case's comparison is unchanged by the cut.

Phase 4 semantics, value namespace only: `let` binds names in the value namespace and must not shadow a function of the same spelling, so `(car (list 1 2))` still resolves the primitive. Fe's `let` primitive takes a bare symbol, so the Emacs-shaped bindings list is a separate, already-divergent shape (primitive-let); the function-cell side of the split is what this case pins. Not flippable with 04C: fe cannot even read the Emacs-shaped bindings list until the prelude's Emacs-shaped `let` exists (04E).

Phase 4 primitive `funcall` (04C): it takes a *value*, here a lexical closure, so the function cell of the name is irrelevant. The funcall machinery itself is complete, but the case's Emacs-shaped `let` bindings list needs the Emacs-shaped `let` (04E), so the comparison cannot run yet.

Sub-plan 04C: a symbol passed to `funcall` is a designator resolved through its function cell, following the same indirection call-position lookup uses, so `(funcall 'g)` calls the fset'd lambda and returns 9. A self-referential chain dies with cyclic-function-indirection rather than exhausting the step budget.

Sub-plan 04C: `apply` spreads its final list argument into the call, so `+` is called with 1 2 3 4 and returns 10. Implemented as an evaluate-then-redispatch on the frame stack (the plan's chosen shape, see doc/implementation.md); a non-list final operand is `apply: last argument must be a proper list`.

Phase 4 primitive `fboundp` (04C) asks the function namespace; the 04D cut moved the bootstrap into function cells, so the primitive `car`'s function cell is occupied and `(fboundp 'car)` is t, matching the 04A-pinned oracle. The pre-cut answer was nil because `car` still lived in a value cell.

Phase 4 designator rule for `functionp`: a symbol whose function cell holds a function is t, an unbound name is nil, never an error. Fe has no `functionp` at all -- it is a kg native that must learn designators when the split lands (04E) -- so the comparison still fails on void-function functionp.

Sub-plan 04C call-position semantics, sharpened by the 04D cut: call position resolves the function cell and an empty cell is void-function -- naming the head symbol -- even when the value cell is full. Reported as FeHandleError()'s message text (the parent plan's message-level rule until Phase 6), which is how the runner matches the oracle's structured void-function condition.

Sub-plan 04C: `symbol-function` returns the function cell's object -- a designator stays a symbol -- and `funcall` calls it, so the roundtrip returns 5. The printed-closure question is avoided by comparing behaviour, per 04A's data decision.

Phase 4 primitive `symbol-value` (04C) reads the value cell directly; the explicit read of a setq'd name agrees, and the mirror arm `lisp2-symbol-value-primitive` passed once the 04D cut emptied the primitive `car`'s value cell, so `(symbol-value 'car)` signals void-variable -- the explicit-value-namespace mirror of one-namespace-boundp's nil.
Sub-plan 04C: `fmakunbound` empties only the function cell, so the subsequent call is void-function j. The pair with the two keeps-* cases pins that the unbound operations act on disjoint cells.
Sub-plan 04C cell separation: `makunbound` acts on the value cell only, leaving the function cell intact, so `(m)` still returns 2. One half of the disjointness the split must preserve.

Sub-plan 04C cell separation, mirror arm: `fmakunbound` leaves the value cell alone, so the bare symbol still evaluates to 1. Together with lisp2-makunbound-keeps-function it records that unbounding one namespace never touches the other.

Sub-plan 04C: `defalias` points one symbol's function cell at another symbol, and call-position resolution follows the designator chain, so `(first (list 1 2))` behaves like `car` and returns 1; `defalias` returns the aliased symbol (first), per the 04A snapshot.

Sub-plan 04C designator rule, timing: function-cell symbol indirection is resolved at call time, not at defalias time -- `a` is aliased to `b` before `b` gets a function, and calling `(a)` afterwards still returns 1. FeGetFunction (the host API, 04C) follows that same chain.

Sub-plan 04C: `(function (lambda ...))` is a raw-form special form producing a real closure value -- not a designator -- and `funcall` calls it directly, returning 3. Since the 04D reader change, `#'(lambda ...)` reads as this same form (reader-sharp-quote-identity).

Sub-plan 04C: `fset` evaluates both arguments -- the first is a value naming the target symbol, not a quote -- so the symbol named by `s` (k) receives the function and `(k)` returns 4. This is the primitive the prelude's 53 setq forms rewrite to in 04E.

kg-policy representation divergence, recorded by Phase 4's own plan (04A): Emacs stores a macro as a (macro . FUNCTION) cons in the function cell, observable only through (symbol-function 'NAME); fe has a distinct FeTMacro type and prints a macro value as (macro PARAMS BODY). Pinned by fe/test_api.c's TestWriter, which already asserts '(macro (a) a)' renders '(macro (a) a)'. The Phase 4 function-cell work (04C) must not imitate the cons representation to pass a case nobody wrote yet; this is kg-policy because Emacs has no anonymous macro object to snapshot at all.
